title: Ideal Gas Equation
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Gas Laws Combined

Boyle, Charles and Gay-Lussac each froze one variable and watched two others. Combine their three laws and out falls PV = nRT — one equation that predicts the pressure, volume or temperature of any (ideal) gas from the other two plus the amount of gas.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2022, 2024)

### 2.1 The three empirical laws

| Law | Statement | Formula (constant) |
|---|---|---|
| **Boyle's law** | At constant T, pressure ∝ 1/volume | $PV = $ const (T, n fixed) |
| **Charles's law** | At constant P, volume ∝ absolute temperature | $V/T = $ const (P, n fixed) |
| **Pressure (Gay-Lussac) law** | At constant V, pressure ∝ absolute temperature | $P/T = $ const (V, n fixed) |

### 2.2 Combining into the ideal gas equation (NEB 2024)

From the three laws, $P \propto T/V$ for fixed n:
$$\frac{P_1V_1}{T_1} = \frac{P_2V_2}{T_2} = \text{const} \Rightarrow \boxed{PV = nRT}$$
- $n$ = number of moles; $R = 8.31$ J mol⁻¹K⁻¹ = **universal gas constant**.
- $R = N_A k_B$; $N_A = 6.022\times10^{23}$ /mol, $k_B = 1.38\times10^{-23}$ J/K.
- In molecular form: $PV = Nk_BT$.
- STP: T = 273.15 K, P = 1.013×10⁵ Pa; molar volume 22.4 L.

### 2.3 Worked numericals

**Q (2m, 2024):** Two moles of an ideal gas at 300 K occupy 0.05 m³. Calculate its pressure. (R = 8.31 J/mol·K)
$$P = \frac{nRT}{V} = \frac{2 \times 8.31 \times 300}{0.05} = 9.97 \times 10^4 \text{ Pa} \approx 1.0 \times 10^5 \text{ Pa}$$

**Q (4m, 2022):** A gas at 27 °C and pressure 1.0×10⁵ Pa occupies 0.5 m³. Find its volume at 100 °C if the pressure remains constant.
- Charles's law: $V_2 = V_1\dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = 0.5 \times \dfrac{373}{300} = 0.62$ m³

**Q (NEB-style):** A gas occupies 2 L at 1 atm and 300 K. Find its volume at 2 atm and 450 K.
$V_2 = V_1 \times \dfrac{P_1}{P_2}\times\dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = 2 \times \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{450}{300} = 1.5$ L.

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 63/64:** kinetic theory derives PV = ⅓Nmv̄² and matches it to PV = NkT — the microscopic origin of the gas laws.
- **To real gases:** the equation holds only at low pressure and high temperature; real gases need van der Waals corrections.
- **To Avogadro:** equal volumes of gases at same T, P contain equal numbers of molecules.

### 4.2 Common examination mistakes

1. Using Celsius temperature in gas laws — always kelvin.
2. Forgetting to convert litres to m³ (1 m³ = 1000 L).
3. Mixing n (moles) with N (molecules): PV = nRT vs PV = NkT.

specificConditions: **Ideal Gas Assumptions:** The equation $PV = nRT$ assumes (1) molecules are point particles with zero volume, (2) no intermolecular forces except during elastic collisions, (3) motion is random and obeys Newton's laws. These hold best at high temperature and low pressure; real gases deviate near condensation.

**Universal Gas Constant:** $R = 8.314 	ext{ J/mol·K}$ is the same for all ideal gases. It connects macroscopic ($P, V, n, T$) to microscopic ($k_B, N_A$) via $R = N_A k_B$. The value depends on units: $R = 0.0821 	ext{ L·atm/mol·K}$ in common chemistry units.

**Temperature Must Be Absolute:** $T$ must be in Kelvin for $PV = nRT$ to hold. Using Celsius gives incorrect results because $T=0^\circ	ext{C} 
eq 0$ kinetic energy. The linear proportionality $P \propto T$ and $V \propto T$ only works with absolute temperature.
